Problem

 Relevance:
The different flavors of the ICON model use a icosahedral-triangular Arakawa C grid which has most variables located in the center of each triangular cell. See here for an example visualization of a coarse global ICON grid.
As of my knowledge most of the people in the atmospheric modeling community rely on interpolation of the unstructured triangle-centered grid to a regular rectilinear lat-lon grid and do not plot the original triangular data.

 Problem Description:
The current functions tricontour/tricontourf require Z to be located on the triangle vertices (x,y) and don't allow triangle-centered data:
tricontour(x, y, Z, levels, triangles=triangles, mask=mask)
tricontourf(x, y, Z, levels, triangles=triangles, mask=mask)
with x,y: (nvertices,) Z: (nvertices,) triangles: (ntri,3) mask: (ntri,)

Now analog to the implemented tripcolor functionality (see 811) allowing triangle-centered data means one of the following to be accepted:
x,y: (nvertices,) Z: (ntri,) triangles: (ntri,3) mask: (ntri,)
or alternatively taking the triangle center locations and optionally maybe neighbor triangle indices for faster computation:
x,y: (ntri,) Z: (ntri,) mask: (ntri,) [neighbors: (ntri,3,)]

One currently possible workaround (but not for masked data) is by letting matplotlib compute the delaunay triangulation of the polygon dual grid which means taking the triangle-centered data coordinates as new vertices of the dual grid. Therefore the following usage is a current workaround:
x,y: (ntri,) Z: (ntri,) triangles: (ntridelaunay,3) mask: (ntridelaunay,)
where for large grids of regular triangles: ntridelaunay ≈ 2 ntri

Masking triangle-centered data is not possible this way because the mask from the data comes in shape (ntri,) and not in the accepted (ntridelaunay,) and alternatively np.nan values are not allowed in Z.

Example plot of tricontourf used with this workaround way with fake data values located on the centers of the yellow triangular grid (=vertices of the black hexagonal dual grid which the delaunay triangulation divides into 4 triangles per hexagon):
 

 Proposed solution

I understood from here how the linear interpolation algorithm along the edges (black in the figure) works but as I don't understand how the currently implemented masking works I can't propose a solution to this, @ianthomas23 maybe you can explain it to us and say something about possibilities. The idea is, not to just exclude the masked data points before delaunay triangulation but to have the contour lines end at the boundaries to the masked triangles (yellow in the figure).
kept_issues.body:
### Problem

### Relevance:
The different flavors of the [ICON model](https://code.mpimet.mpg.de/projects/iconpublic) use a icosahedral-triangular Arakawa C grid which has most variables located in the center of each triangular cell. See [here](https://www.dwd.de/EN/research/weatherforecasting/num_modelling/bilder/01b_icon_r2b04_orographie_en.png) for an example visualization of a coarse global ICON grid.
As of my knowledge most of the people in the atmospheric modeling community rely on interpolation of the unstructured triangle-centered grid to a regular rectilinear lat-lon grid and do not plot the original triangular data.

### Problem Description:
The current functions tricontour/tricontourf require Z to be located on the triangle vertices (x,y) and don't allow triangle-centered data:
`tricontour(x, y, Z, levels, triangles=triangles, mask=mask)`
`tricontourf(x, y, Z, levels, triangles=triangles, mask=mask)`
with **x,y: (nvertices,)  Z: (nvertices,)  triangles: (ntri,3)  mask: (ntri,)**

Now analog to the implemented tripcolor functionality (see #811) allowing triangle-centered data means one of the following to be accepted:
**x,y: (nvertices,)  Z: (ntri,)  triangles: (ntri,3)  mask: (ntri,)**
or alternatively taking the triangle center locations and optionally maybe neighbor triangle indices for faster computation:
**x,y: (ntri,)  Z: (ntri,)  mask: (ntri,) [neighbors: (ntri,3,)]**


One currently possible workaround (but not for masked data) is by letting matplotlib compute the delaunay triangulation of the polygon dual grid which means taking the triangle-centered data coordinates as new vertices of the dual grid. Therefore the following usage is a current workaround:
**x,y: (ntri,)  Z: (ntri,)  triangles: (ntridelaunay,3)  mask: (ntridelaunay,)**
where for large grids of regular triangles: ntridelaunay ≈ 2 * ntri

Masking triangle-centered data is not possible this way because the mask from the data comes in shape (ntri,) and not in the accepted (ntridelaunay,) and alternatively np.nan values are not allowed in Z.

Example plot of tricontourf used with this workaround way with fake data values located on the centers of the yellow triangular grid (=vertices of the black hexagonal dual grid which the delaunay triangulation divides into 4 triangles per hexagon):
![tricontourf_trianlge_centered_data_workaround](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/48184906/172461913-b507bf73-0fa5-400f-87c3-7f06d122e1fa.png)



### Proposed solution

I understood from [here](https://discourse.matplotlib.org/t/how-precise-could-tricontourf-be/22220) how the linear interpolation algorithm along the edges (black in the figure) works but as I don't understand how the currently implemented masking works I can't propose a solution to this, @ianthomas23 maybe you can explain it to us and say something about possibilities. The idea is, not to just exclude the masked data points before delaunay triangulation but to have the contour lines end at the boundaries to the masked triangles (yellow in the figure).
kept_issues.title: [ENH]: Allow tricontour and tricontourf to plot masked triangle-centered data

kept_issues.body:
### Problem

Currently, motion_notify_event generates a MouseEvent with a `.button` attribute that is generated by dead-reckoning: it fills that value by tracking button_press_events and button_release_events.  This means that the value can be wrong (if the user starts pressing a button (keeping it pressed), moves the mouse out of the canvas, presses another button, releases the first one, moves back over the canvas), and also this cannot represent the case of multiple buttons being pressed (for a motion_notify_event, the main thing that makes sense to report is really "what are all pressed buttons", not "what was the last pressed button").

### Proposed solution

Similarly to #23473, one could add a `.buttons` attribute (a frozenset of MouseButtons) to MouseEvents (well, at least to those generated by motion_notify_event) and fill that accordingly, as UI toolkits typically report that info (e.g. https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qsinglepointevent.html#buttons, compare with https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qsinglepointevent.html#button).

I think (assuming we can get #23473 in, which would mean we agree on this kind of API) we can tag this "good first issue"/"medium" as the new API would be well-defined but the work requires understanding various UI toolkits.
kept_issues.title: [ENH]: Add buttons (plural) attribute to mouseevents

### Proposed solution

I while ago, I wrote a helper function to generate ticks and labels. It's not pretty (and not optimal either), but it works.
```
import fractions
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

def _labels_and_ticks(first, last, step, symbol=r'\pi', symval=np.pi):
    try:
        s_num, s_den = symbol.split('/')
    except ValueError:
        s_num = symbol
        s_den = '1'
    coefficients = np.arange(first, last + step / 2, step)

    labels = []
    for i, coefficient in enumerate(coefficients):
        value = fractions.Fraction(coefficient).limit_denominator()
        num = value.numerator
        den = value.denominator

        # Case 1: `coefficient` is zero.
        if not num:
            labels.append('$0$')
            continue

        # Case 2: `coefficient` is non-zero.
        builder = ['$']
        if num < 0:
            builder.append('-')
            num = abs(num)
        is_fraction = den != 1 or s_den != '1'
        if is_fraction:
            builder.append(r'\dfrac{')
        if num != 1:
            builder.append(f'{num}')
        if s_num != '1' or num == 1:
            builder.append(s_num)
        if is_fraction:
            builder.append(r'}{')
        if den != 1:
            builder.append(f'{den}')
        if s_den != '1':
            builder.append(s_den)
        if is_fraction:
            builder.append(r'}')
        builder.append('$')
        labels.append(''.join(builder))
    return (labels, symval * coefficients)

(fig, ax) = plt.subplots()
labels, ticks = _labels_and_ticks(-2, 2, 0.25)
ax.set_xticks(ticks, labels)
x = np.linspace(-2 * np.pi, 2 * np.pi, 1000)
y = np.sin(x)
ax.plot(x, y)
ax.grid(True)
plt.show()
```
![sin2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/19171016/183255133-4fcd98e6-b669-49ea-b34e-5d087e5a6605.png)

It can also handle fractions.
```
(fig, ax) = plt.subplots()
labels, ticks = _labels_and_ticks(-2, 2, 1/6, r'\pi/\gamma', np.pi/np.euler_gamma)
ax.set_xticks(ticks, labels)
x = np.linspace(-2 * np.pi / np.euler_gamma, 2 * np.pi / np.euler_gamma, 1000)
y = np.sin(np.euler_gamma * x)
ax.plot(x, y)
ax.grid(True)
plt.show()
```
![sin3](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/19171016/183255286-8a0dcd36-75af-491e-a210-7ca5a5675ee0.png)

Would be nice to have this feature in Matplotlib.
kept_issues.title: [ENH]: Coordinate axes ticks at multiples of a number (like π)

 Proposed solution

@timhoffm raised the good point that we don't want to break the artist-(label, handle) link in case the artist gets updated, so I think an alternative solution is maybe to have this logic in the legend. Something like a duplicate keyword argument to legend:

 , default, current behavior
 - triggers a check of legend objects. If multiple legend handles have the same properties (class, color/edgecolor, hatch, size/width/edgewidth, etc) and the same label, then a new handle with those properties linked to all the artists is shown in place of the original handles.

I'm not sure if this is even doable in the current architecture, but if possible this would be designed so that updates to properties that update handles/legends propagate back to create new entries on the legend as needed. The advantage of this approach is that it would facilitate explicitly linking legend labels & handles to multiple artists. 

I think currently duplicates are eliminated manually either by omitting the labels on some artists or creating a custom legend handle. Neither approach preserves a link between a legend entry and all the artists it is intended to describe.

For example, the blue signal in zoom out is represented incorrectly:

 
 

One problem is also that signals are overlapping, but this could be possibly improved as follows:

 Proposed solution

Assuming we have an array x = [x0, x1, ... xn] and view area v = [v0, v1, ... vm] for m < n, and assuming k points from v are merged into x. Then one option of compacting the x into v, would be:

- definitely when compacting the signals intensity should change to notify visually that in "that segment" there is some spread, and it would be possible to see "spikes" from large data-sets in zoomed-out images.

kept_issues.body:
### Problem

In Matplotlib 3, when using a list of values for the `levels` argument in `contour()`, the list of values is overridden in the case that all requested levels fall outside the data range. While this may be desirable for casually browsing data when the user is unfamiliar with the data range, it causes serious problems for batch applications where the user legitimately intends to use their list of levels but does not know whether every input array will produce contours.

Example:
```
myplot = plt.contour( x , y , data , levels = [100] )
print( myplot.levels )
```

The above prints `[0.0]` when `data` is an array of values ranging from 0 to 50 (i.e., the requested contour level of 100 is outside the data range). As a result, the plot contains erroneous contours around near-zero values, presumably due to floating point precision.

This is a consequence of the change described here (https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/prev_api_changes/api_changes_3.0.0.html?highlight=contour%20levels):

> Selection of contour levels is now the same for contour and contourf; previously, for contour, levels outside the data range were deleted. **(Exception: if no contour levels are found within the data range, the levels attribute is replaced with a list holding only the minimum of the data range.)**

### Proposed solution

Add a kwarg to `contour()` that overrides the autoscaling behavior. When the kwarg is set, it would trigger a flag in `_process_contour_level_args()` (https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/blob/main/lib/matplotlib/contour.py):

```
if not self.filled:
            inside = (self.levels > self.zmin) & (self.levels < self.zmax)
            levels_in = self.levels[inside]
            if len(levels_in) == 0 and not(OVERRIDE_AUTOSCALE_FLAG):
                self.levels = [self.zmin]
                _api.warn_external(
                    "No contour levels were found within the data range.")
```
kept_issues.title: [ENH]: Allow override of contour level autoscaling

kept_issues.body:
### Problem

When using `pyplot.arrow`, the coordinates `x, y, dx, dy` are within the same coordinate system than the styling kwargs, resulting in different appearances, when used on multiple plots with different scales.

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axs = plt.subplots(nrows=3, layout='constrained')

for ii, ax in enumerate(axs.flat):

    ax.set_xlim( [ ii/5, 1 - ii/5 ] )
    ax.set_ylim( [ .5 - (ii+1)/50, .5 + (ii+1)/50 ] )

    ax.arrow( 1 - ii/5, .5, 2 * ii/5 - 1, 0, length_includes_head=True, linewidth=0, width=.01 )
```

![arrows](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7861774/197810373-fb3466bd-7c24-4590-92f2-1363e2c5cc09.jpg)

`transform=ax.transAxes` transforms both, placement and appearance, resulting in homogeneous appearance and hard to handle placement.

![arrows2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7861774/197811685-7e2e26ca-5114-4f82-aa09-8eacec374ad0.jpg)



### Proposed solution

Having coordinates `x, y, dx, dy` in data coordinates and styling kwargs in axes coordinates.

(And `length_includes_head=True` as default *cough*)
kept_issues.title: [ENH]: Scale Invariant Arrow Styling

kept_issues.body:
### Problem

Currently, if one wants to draw multiple categories of bars side-by-side as in https://matplotlib.org/devdocs/gallery/lines_bars_and_markers/barchart.html, one has to calculate the bar positions manually. This is really a nuissance and too low level for any user-facing interface. Actually, when asked I recommend to use pandas plotting functions for that if possible, which is really embarrasing.

There have been stalled attempts to do this (issure 10610, PR #11048). Additionally, this often gets related to a function for stacked bars #14086.



### Proposed solution

I'd like to pick up this topic and come up with a reasonable API. This topic is really complex and one can easily get lost in various details. For the design procedure, I take a bottom-up appoach by starting with a basic function `grouped_bar()` that does only expose the minimal functionality to get the plot done. I then intended to additional parameters one by one as they fit in. - So don't be concerned that the first proposal here is quite basic.

**Terminology** I'll use *label* for the x-values, i.e. 'G1' .. 'G5' in above example, and *group* for the categories, i.e. 'Tea'/'Coffee'.

---

###  For now: Only vertical orientation
I'll limit the discussion here to 'vertical'. We can have a separate discussion whether we want to add an *orientation* parameter or make a `grouped_barh`. Both are technically easy and only an API design decision that's orthogonal to the rest of the API.

### For now: Only grouped layout, no stacked layout
To keep things simple, I'll limit myself to grouped for now, because:
- Stacked is somewhat simpler than grouped as you only need to insert the *bottom* values in multiple calls. For two bars it's just the heights of the firsts, and a cumsum for more than two.
- We may build a separate `stacked_bar()` function, if the first bullet point is considered too cumbersome.
- It's conceivable to unite both in one function as poposed in #11048 and realized in `DataFrame.plot.bar`, but that needs careful additional consideration.

either way let's defer stacked bars to later.

### Minimal API

We want to be able to rewrite https://matplotlib.org/devdocs/gallery/lines_bars_and_markers/barchart.html as

```
grouped_bar(labels, [tea_means, coffee_means], group_labels=['Tea', 'Coffee']) 
```

Thus, the minimal API is:

```
def grouped_bar(x, heights, *, group_labels=None):
    """
    Parameters
    -----------
    x : array-like of str
         The labels.
    heights : list of array-like:
         An iterable of array-like: The iteration runs over the groups.
         Each individual array-like is the list of label values for that group.
    group_labels : array-like of str, optional
         The labels of the data groups.
    """
```

---

I'll soon expand on the minimal API, answering a lot of questions from https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/pull/11048#issuecomment-381812675. But before that, please speak up in case you have fundamental concerns with adding such functionality at all or with the bottom-up design approach. OTOH if you think this is worth pursuing, please give a :+1:.
kept_issues.title: [ENH]: API discussion for grouped bar charts

kept_issues.body:
### Problem

Trying to combine subplot_mosaic with axes using various different projections (e.g. one rectilinear axes and one polar axes and one 3d axes) has been requested a few times (once in the original subplot_mosaic thread IIRC, and in #20392 too), and it's something I would recently have been happy to have, too.

Pushing projections directly into subplot_mosaic seems ripe for API bloat, but perhaps another solution would be to add `figure.gridspec_mosaic(...)` which takes the same arguments as subplot_mosaic, but returns a dict of *subplotspecs*, such that one can do something like
```
specs = fig.gridspec_mosaic(...)
d = {
    "foo": fig.add_subplot(specs["foo"], projection=...),
    "bar": fig.add_subplot(specs["bar"], projection=...),
    ...
}
```
As a side point, I do find the repetition of `fig` in each call to add_subplot a bit jarring (as the underlying gridspec is bound to the figure, so that information is actually redundant).  Back in #13280 I had proposed to add SubplotSpec.add_subplot() (adding to the figure to which the gridspec is bound), which would allow one to write, here,
```
specs = fig.gridspec_mosaic(...)
d = {
    "foo": specs["foo"].add_subplot(projection=...),
    "bar": specs["bar"].add_subplot(projection=...),
    ...
}
```
but that idea got shot down back then and even if we decide not to revisit it, even the first form would be nice to have.

Thoughts?

### Proposed solution

_No response_

kept_issues.body:
### Problem

Despite our advice (https://matplotlib.org/stable/tutorials/introductory/quick_start.html#making-a-helper-functions ) a large number of down stream libraries create Figures on behalf of users and do not provide a way for the user to pass in either the Figure or Axes that they would like to have their data plotted to.  A couple times a year we have requests like https://gitter.im/matplotlib/matplotlib?at=63b81c09c9591d20d38d6c5c where users are trapped by functions from down stream libraries that can not be composed the way they want.

In that thread I suggested the user (at their own risk) monkey patch `plt.subplots` as a pragmatic solution, but after a couple of iterations this turned into something that seemed reasonable for use to implement upstream.

### Proposed solution

The core problem here is that the user wants to inject some state through a call stack that does not provide a way to thread that state through (e.g. the plotting methods do not take `ax` or `fig`) so that leaves us with using global state to pass this through.  Fortunately in Python modules _are_ global state and the way pyplot is built we have exactly one entry point for fabricating new `Figure` objects so if we wanted to do something like say "the next 4 times I create a new Figure please _actually_ give me the SubFigures from a 2x2 grid" we can do that as:

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from contextlib import contextmanager


@contextmanager
def monkey_patch_figure(nrows, ncols, fig_kargs=None, **subfig_kwargs):
    fig_kargs = fig_kargs or {}
    orig_figure = plt.figure

    outer_fig = orig_figure(**fig_kargs)
    fig_iter = iter(outer_fig.subfigures(nrows, ncols, **subfig_kwargs).ravel())

    def patch_figure(*args, **kwargs):
        print('called')
        if args or kwargs:
            # TODO make actual warning or raise?
            print(f"got non-empty {args=} or {kwargs=} which will be ignored")
        return next(fig_iter)

    plt.figure = patch_figure

    try:
        yield outer_fig
    finally:
        plt.figure = orig_figure

with monkey_patch_figure(2, 2) as fig:
    plt.subplots(1, 2)
    plt.plot(range(5))
    plt.subplots(3, 1)
    plt.plot(range(5))
    plt.subplot_mosaic('AA;BC')
    plt.plot(range(5))
    plt.subplots()
    plt.plot(range(5))    

```

If we were to pull this into Matplotlib we probably should have the context manager set some private state that `plt.figure` looks at to decide if it should mint a new Figure or pop one off the stack (to catch downstream libraries who have done `from matplotlib.pyplot import figure` or `from pylab import *`) 

This works for the minimal smoke testing in the example so I'm sure that there are a bunch of edge cases that do not work as expected.  I think there a couple of decision points here:

1. is this even a good idea? On one hand it appears to solve a long standing problem ..... by using more of that problem (global state and the application-ness / statefullness of pyplot).
2. is patching `plt.figure` the right place?  The first iteration of this thinking patched `subplots` (and should do `subplot_moasic` as well).  The pro of `figure` is that it is broader so will catch more uses, but the con is because it is broader it will get more uses which makes it more likely we will hit edge cases that break.
3. Should this go in core or get shuffled off to mpl-gui / some other third-party packaging (or just be documented (or is this issue enough)?
kept_issues.title: [ENH]: context manager to hijack down stream creation of new Figures

Problem

Plotting data in subplots can sometimes be a pain. For instance, if you want to create one plot for each day of the year.
 
Note that the number of days can change according to the year, it is not easy to find a good grid that fits all the data. You also need to hide the tiles that remain unused. Additionally, if you have too many rows, this method will not display the tick labels for the bottom-most plots (because they are not the last row). Finally, there are many points where errors can be made, potentially leading to unexpected results.

 Proposed solution

It would be far more convenient to have an easy way to sequentially plot.
One could start a subplot object that contains zero plots.
Then you add plots in a sequential manner. You get a row vector with plots and a linear index (for instance, 0 to len - 1).
Once you are done making the plots, you can call a function that will produce the layout. You may pass the number of columns and rows for this layout and how to fill (by column or row). You then can show or save the figure.

Example code:

 
Providing a too little width x height after creating the tiles throws an error.
The layout can be built in advance too, in this case there is only width x height tiles available.
If there are new tiles, the layout adds a row or column according to the fill_by argument.

By default fill_by fills by row:
0 1 2 3
4 5 6 7
...

Alternatively, one can fill by column:
0 4
1 5
2 6
3 7
...

One could give either height or width and the counterpart could be calculated automatically
For instance:
tile.layout(height = 21, fill_by = 'row')
Calculates the smallest number for width:
width = math.ceil(len(tiles)/height)

There could be a default height and width that could be calculated using sqrt of the length of tiles
 

Only the last width tiles would have the x-axis displayed, the other tiles have it hidden by default
The missing tiles in the width x height layout are by default hidden.
kept_issues.body:
### Problem

Plotting data in subplots can sometimes be a pain. For instance, if you want to create one plot for each day of the year.
```
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def days_in_year(year):
    return (np.datetime64(f'{(year+1)}-01-01')-np.datetime64(f'{(year)}-01-01')).astype(int)

print(days_in_year(2013)) # 365 days
print(days_in_year(2012)) # 366 days
print(days_in_year(2014)) # 365 days

# 21*18 >= 366
n_cols = 18
n_rows = 21

fig, axs = plt.subplots(n_cols, n_rows,  sharex = True,  sharey = True)

for d in range(days_in_year(2013)):
    x = np.random.rand(20)
    y = np.random.rand(20)
    
    # calculate the plot location
    col = d % n_cols # prone to error
    row = int(d/n_cols) # prone to error

    # plot
    axs[col,row].scatter(x,y) # again, prone to error row,col vs col,row

plt.show()
```
Note that the number of days can change according to the year, it is not easy to find a good grid that fits all the data. You also need to hide the tiles that remain unused. Additionally, if you have too many rows, this method will not display the tick labels for the bottom-most plots (because they are not the last row). Finally, there are many points where errors can be made, potentially leading to unexpected results.

### Proposed solution

It would be far more convenient to have an easy way to sequentially plot.
One could start a subplot object that contains zero plots.
Then you add plots in a sequential manner. You get a row vector with plots and a linear index (for instance, 0 to len - 1).
Once you are done making the plots, you can call a function that will produce the layout. You may pass the number of columns and rows for this layout and how to fill (by column or row). You then can show or save the figure.

Example code:

```
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def days_in_year(year):
    return (np.datetime64(f'{(year+1)}-01-01')-np.datetime64(f'{(year)}-01-01')).astype(int)

print(days_in_year(2013)) # 365 days
print(days_in_year(2012)) # 366 days
print(days_in_year(2014)) # 365 days

tile = plt.tiled(sharex = True,  sharey = True)

for d in range(days_in_year(2013)):
    x = np.random.rand(20)
    y = np.random.rand(20)
    
    tile.nexttile()

    # plots in the current tile
    tile.scatter(x,y)

tile.tile[2].plot([0, 0], [0, 1]) # add a plot to an existing tile

tile.layout(height = 21, width= 18, fill_by = 'row') 
plt.show()
```
Providing a too little width x height after creating the tiles throws an error.
The layout can be built in advance too, in this case there is only width x height tiles available.
If there are new tiles, the layout adds a row or column according to the fill_by argument.

By default fill_by fills by row:
0 1 2 3
4 5 6 7
...

Alternatively, one can fill by column:
0 4
1 5
2 6
3 7
...

One could give either height or width and the counterpart could be calculated automatically
For instance:
`tile.layout(height = 21, fill_by = 'row')`
Calculates the smallest number for width:
`width = math.ceil(len(tiles)/height)`

There could be a default height and width that could be calculated using sqrt of the length of tiles
```
width = math.ceil(sqrt(len(tiles)))
height = math.floor(sqrt(len(tiles)))
``` 

Only the last width tiles would have the x-axis displayed, the other tiles have it hidden by default
The missing tiles in the width x height layout are by default hidden.
kept_issues.title: [ENH]: Include something equivalent to Matlab's tiledlayout and nexttile

_api.check_isinstance((Normalize, None), norm=norm)

_api.check_isinstance((Normalize, str, None), norm=norm)

Problem

I became frustrated trying to get consistent figures. I wanted to scale them according to the limits on the x and/or y axes, and sometimes set fixed axes width/height, margins, and subplot spacing.

 Proposed solution
kept_issues.body:
### Problem

I became frustrated trying to get consistent figures. I wanted to scale them according to the limits on the x and/or y axes, and sometimes set fixed axes width/height, margins, and subplot spacing.

I've written a convenient function to allow me to control these elements. It works great for my purposes, and I thought it could be helpful to adapt and include in the code base. Let me know if I'm an idiot and this already exists.

### Proposed solution

```python
def set_figure_size(self, fig, axes,
                    height_ax_rel=None, width_ax_rel=None,
                    width_ax_in=None, height_ax_in=None,
                    height_gap_in=None, width_gap_in=None,
                    top_in=None, bottom_in=None,
                    left_in=None, right_in=None):
    """Sets figure and axes elements to fixed sizes. Assumes a 2-D
    axes array, that axes sharex and sharey, and in a regular grid
    pattern.

    Args:
        fig (matplotlib.pyplot.figure): matplotlib figure to adjust
        axes (2D numpy.ndarray): matplotlib axes array for sizing
        height_ax_rel (float, optional): axis unit to inches ratio for the
            y-axis.
        width_ax_rel (float, optional): axis unit to inches ration for the
            x-axis.
        width_ax_in (float, optional): fixed width of each axis in inches
        height_ax_in (float, optional): fixed height of each axis in inches
        width_gap_in (float, optional): fixed width of gaps between each
            axis in inches
        height_gap_in (float, optional): fixed height of gaps between each
            axis in inches
        top_in (float, optional): fixed height of top margin in inches
        bottom_in (float, optional): fixed height of bottom margin in inches
        left_in (float, optional): fixed width of left margin in inches
        right_in (float, optional): fixed width of right margin in inches
    """
    ax = axes[0, 0]
    rows, cols = axes.shape

    if width_ax_in is None:
        # x limits of axes
        left_ax, right_ax = ax.get_xlim()
        # width of axes in inches
        width_ax_in = (right_ax - left_ax) * width_ax_rel
    if width_gap_in is None:
        # get width from relative width * axis width
        width_gap_in = fig.subplotpars.wspace * width_ax_in
    else:
        # set relative width to gap:axis ratio
        fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=width_gap_in/width_ax_in)
    # comput subplot width
    width_subplot_in = width_gap_in * (cols - 1) + width_ax_in * cols
    if right_in is None:
        # get right margin size from relative size * subplot size
        right_in = (1 - fig.subplotpars.right) * width_subplot_in
    else:
        # set relative right side position to 1 - margin:subplot ratio
        fig.subplots_adjust(right=1-(right_in/(right_in+width_subplot_in)))
    if left_in is None:
        # get left margin size from relative size * subplot size
        left_in = fig.subplotpars.left * width_subplot_in
    else:
        # set relative left side position to margin:subplot ratio
        fig.subplots_adjust(left=left_in/(left_in+width_subplot_in))
    width_fig_in = left_in + width_subplot_in + right_in

    # repeat the process for figure height
    if height_ax_in is None:
        bottom_ax, top_ax = ax.get_ylim()
        height_ax_in = (top_ax - bottom_ax) * height_ax_rel
    if height_gap_in is None:
        height_gap_in = fig.subplotpars.hspace * height_ax_in
    else:
        fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=height_gap_in/height_ax_in)
    height_subplot_in = height_gap_in * (rows - 1) + height_ax_in * rows
    if top_in is None:
        top_in = (1 - fig.subplotpars.top) * height_subplot_in
    else:
        fig.subplots_adjust(top=1-(top_in/(top_in+height_subplot_in)))
    if bottom_in is None:
        bottom_in = fig.subplotpars.bottom * height_subplot_in
    else:
        fig.subplots_adjust(bottom=bottom_in/(bottom_in+height_subplot_in))
    height_fig_in = top_in + height_subplot_in + bottom_in

    fig.set_size_inches(width_fig_in, height_fig_in)
```
kept_issues.title: [ENH]: Setting figure margins, subplot gaps, and axis sizes to fixed values in inches

kept_issues.body:
### Problem

When `x` is 1D and `y` is 2D, the expression `plot(x, y)` behaves differently in Matplotlib and MATLAB. Matplotlib requires that `y.shape[0] == x.size` and always plots the columns of `y` against `x`. MATLAB will plot by `y` by columns if its first dimension is compatible with `x`, but if it is not, and the second dimension of `y` *is* compatible with `x`, then it will plot `y` by rows. 

The following code works in MATLAB, for example:
```Matlab
x = linspace(0, 2*pi);    % Size: [1 x 100]
k = (0:2)';               % Size: [3 x 1]
y = sin(k*x);             % Size: [3 x 100]
plot(x, y)                % Second dimensions are the same
plot(x, y')               % Second dimension of x is the same as first dimension of y'
```
In the similar code below, Matplotlib returns an error for `plot(x, y)`, but not for `plot(x, y.T)`:
```python
x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi)    # Shape: (50,)
k = np.arange(3).                # Shape: (3,)
y = np.sin(np.outer(k, x))       # Shape: (3, 50)
plt.plot(x, y)                   # Returns ValueError
plt.plot(x, y.T)                 # y.T has shape (50, 3), compatible with x
```
The NumPy broadcasting rules and FFT routines are organized around row operations, which forces a choice between rows and columns—see [here](https://discourse.matplotlib.org/t/plotting-rows-of-a-2d-array-tension-between-matplotlib-and-numpy-broadcasting-inconsistency-with-matlab/23778?u=jsdodge) for an example.

### Proposed solution

When `x` is 1D and `y` is 2D, plot `y` by columns when `y.shape[0] == x.size`, but also try to plot `y` by rows when `y.shape[0] != x.size`.
kept_issues.title: [ENH]: Expand shape compatibility of x and y in plot

kept_issues.body:
### Problem

As of matplotlib 3.7, `matplotlib.colors.SymLogNorm` instances expose their `linthresh` parameter publicly, but not their `base`, though it is still possible to retrieve it via private attributes. For illustration:

```python
from matplotlib.colors import SymLogNorm

sln = sln = SymLogNorm(linthresh=1, base=5)
print(f"{sln.linthresh=}, {sln._trf.base=}") 
```
outputs
```
sln.linthresh=1, sln._trf.base=5
```

yt has custom routines to determine colorbar ticks for symlog norms, so it needs to know how the norm was parametrised.
At the moment there is no public API to retrieve the `base` parameter, so it cannot be done in a future-proof fashion.

### Proposed solution

It suffices to re-expose the attribute as is already done for `linthresh`

```patch
diff --git a/lib/matplotlib/colors.py b/lib/matplotlib/colors.py
index 434bb54235..f4939fd1a7 100644
--- a/lib/matplotlib/colors.py
+++ b/lib/matplotlib/colors.py
@@ -1844,6 +1844,14 @@ class SymLogNorm(Normalize):
     def linthresh(self, value):
         self._scale.linthresh = value

+    @property
+    def base(self):
+        return self._trf.base
+
+    @base.setter
+    def base(self, value):
+        self._trf.base = value
+

 @make_norm_from_scale(
     scale.AsinhScale,
```

would this change be acceptable ?
kept_issues.title: [ENH]: could there be a long-term stable API to access the log base from a SymLogNorm object ?

kept_issues.body:
### Problem

I would like to be able to call a `plt.subplots` type function that creates a figure and axes that best maintains a desired figure shape. Basically a function that nicely tiles  `nsubplots` in a figure.

### Proposed solution

A very basic solution would be something like the following:

```
def create_subplots(nsubplots, ratio=.5, overflow_cols=True):
    nrows = int(round(nsubplots ** ratio))
    ncols = int(round(nsubplots ** (1-ratio)))
    if nrows * ncols < nsubplots:
        if overflow_cols:
            ncols += 1
        else:
            nrows += 1
    fig = plt.figure()
    axs = [fig.add_subplot(nrows,ncols,i+1) for i in range(nsubplots)]
    return fig, axs             
```
And of course other arguments should be able to be used similar to the keyword arguments of `plt.subplots`. I think somehow incorporating `width_ratios` and `height_ratios` would make this very useful.

This may not be a problem in some situations, such as when one is actually creating a dedicated plot, but for, e.g., an extension it would be nice if there was a way to either propagate the cycler (and get the results) or be able to share cycler (or just do something like `axes2.set_prop_cycle(axes1.get_prop_cycle())`. 

### Proposed solution

Add a public way to get the next cycle results and/or enable linking/sharing cycler (where the cycler is defined in e.g. styles, so "unknown" to the user).

kept_issues._normalized_body:
Problem

Is there any prospect of adding some high-level methods that would simply allow adding subplots to a figure without implicitly having to know the total number of subplots to be plotted and specify their exact layout in advance?
This issue is closely related to the request for a way to dynamically make new subplots on the fly, the lack of which has been another plight for some time. Methods of solving that, including the common hack using gridspec and set_subplotspec to reposition all the axes each time you add a new plot, would probably solve the issue at hand too as they obviously don’t require knowing the number of subplots beforehand.

This issue is more general though and I would expect it has a wider range of solutions, but currently the only workaround I can think of (but haven’t tried yet) would be to make a figure and then continuously add subplots using ax = fig.add_subplot() to the same default position (1, 1, 1), and then iterate through fig.axes() at the end, using gridspec and set_subplotspec to rearrange the plots, similar to the above hack for dynamic plotting.

If you want an example use case that would give rise to this issue, imagine you have multiple data sets which you are about to process.
1. The processing involves splitting and merging datasets, and plotting whatever datasets fulfil a bunch of nested if statements, the number of which you have no idea.
2. These datasets get plotted using various different types of plots (and hence using different matplotlib methods) depending on which if statements they fulfil, there being more possible types than you care to count.
3. The datasets are processed in a loop that reassigns the same variables in each iteration and you don’t want to retain much data in memory after each iteration.

(1) means that it’s not simply a case of calculating the size of your dataframe or whatever to know the number of plots (a common theme in examples) – the conditional logic means you really only know how many plots you’ve got after you go through it. (2) does away with any idea of storing the parameters of each plot in a dictionary and all dictionaries in a list to go through after you've figured out exactly what your plotting, as you don’t even know which plotting method you’re going to use and it’s not feasible to make a custom map by which to identify them, besides the clunkiness involved when you’ve got a lot of axis options you want to configure. (3) makes it undesirable anyway to be retaining anything in memory beyond what’s necessary for the plot itself and any derived quantities etc you want to keep.

 Proposed solution

The problem might lie with axes being inseparably tied since their formation to figures, and there being no trivial way to adjust the size and layout of a figure after its formation. One possible solution might therefore lie in adding the ability to make axes independent of figures, configure all axes-specific options and then add them to figures using fig.add_subplot(). Another would be if new subplots can be added using knowledge of only the current number of axes, so something like fig.add_subplot(len(fig.axes)+1, 1, len(fig.axes)+1) to add a new subplot on the end of a single column of plots, upon running of which the size and other necessary components of the figure are automatically adjusted in the background without the user having to do that manually. The latter could also solve the dynamic plotting issue.

I’m guessing modifying the inner workings of matplotlib.figure would yield an optimal solution for this, but even a native wrapper around the gridspec and set_subplotspec technique could at least save beginners significant time and effort for what doesn’t appear to be a particularly advanced task worth getting stuck on: simply adding subplots without knowing their total number from the outset.

Problem

Trying to plot a volume inside a volume, with one ax.voxels call, doesn't seem possible:

 Proposed solution

kept_issues.body:
### Problem

Trying to plot a volume inside a volume, with one `ax.voxels` call, doesn't seem possible:

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from matplotlib import colors

inner = np.zeros((4, 4, 4), dtype=bool)
inner[1:3, 1:3, 1:3] = 1
outer = np.ones((4, 4, 4), dtype=bool)
voxelarray = inner | outer

facecolors = np.empty(voxelarray.shape + (4,), dtype=object)
facecolors[outer] = colors.to_rgba("blue", alpha=0.5)
facecolors[inner] = colors.to_rgba("red")

fig = plt.figure()
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")
ax.voxels(voxelarray, facecolors=facecolors)
fig.savefig("nested_volumes.png")
```

![nested volumes one voxels call](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/assets/8990777/de14cc81-a5c3-4d3f-99f6-4e3fa611ea9f)

Nest volumes are possible if invoking `ax.voxels` twice:

```python
outer_facecolors = np.empty(outer.shape + (4,), dtype=object)
outer_facecolors[outer] = colors.to_rgba("blue", alpha=0.5)
inner_facecolors = np.empty(inner.shape, dtype=object)
inner_facecolors[inner] = "red"

fig = plt.figure()
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection="3d")
ax.voxels(outer, facecolors=outer_facecolors)
ax.voxels(inner, facecolors=inner_facecolors)
ax.set_axis_off()
plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("nested_volumes.png", transparent=True)
```

![nested volumes individual voxels call](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/assets/8990777/de2c0ab2-34c7-4eec-8dd4-98f1a845de66)


### Proposed solution

It would be nice if `matplotlib` supported `alpha` with `voxels` for nested volumes.

Related: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/48672663/matplotlib-render-all-internal-voxels-with-alpha, which leads to the dupe https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/issues/9745 that was closed due to inactivity
kept_issues.title: [ENH]: nested volumes with one `ax.voxels` call using `alpha`

---

 Problem

In (v3.6) we prohibited negative errors to bring the behavior in line with the documentation.

I've got the request to again support negative errors, so that the error bar can be detached from the marker. There seem to be cases where users exactly want this behavior, e.g.

 

 Proposed solution

I think we should support this somehow. Possibilities:

- Revert to the old behavior and adjust the documentation accordingly. I'm not clear whether not allowing negative errors was really a conscious decision or whether we were only making the code behave according to the documentation. - Technically, negative errors are perfictly fine. The only justification I see for the positive error limitation is to enforce a more narrow semantics that errors are usually positive and we want to guard users against accidental negative errors. 
- Alternatively, we could introduce an explicit allow_negative_errors flag.

Choosing between those, I'm inclined to say that the flag feels a bit cumbersome and we can assume that users are responsible enough to handle their data without us needing to enforce negative errors. After all, even if they are undesired, it should be relatively easy to spot and find out the reason.

### Problem

In https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/pull/21266 (v3.6) we prohibited negative errors to bring the behavior in line with the documentation.

I've got the request to again support negative errors, so that the error bar can be detached from the marker. There seem to be cases where users exactly want this behavior, e.g.

![image](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/assets/2836374/1a3a0bd1-cce4-4383-9e05-a5c111757164)



### Proposed solution

I think we should support this somehow. Possibilities:

- Revert to the old behavior and adjust the documentation accordingly. I'm not clear whether not allowing negative errors was really a conscious decision or whether we were only making the code behave according to the documentation. - Technically, negative errors are perfictly fine. The only justification I see for the positive error limitation is to enforce a more narrow semantics that errors are usually positive and we want to guard users against accidental negative errors. 
- Alternatively, we could introduce an explicit `allow_negative_errors` flag.

Choosing between those, I'm inclined to say that the flag feels a bit cumbersome and we can assume that users are responsible enough to handle their data without us needing to enforce negative errors. After all, even if they are undesired, it should be relatively easy to spot and find out the reason.

Plotting a 2-dim histogram using the hist2d function can leave a lot of excess space in the plot when using the argument cmin to exclude bins with insufficient numbers of data-points. (There's presumably a similar problem when using the argument cmax).

 import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

 size = 100000
 x = rng.normal(scale=10, size=size)
 y = rng.normal(size=size)

 This plot has properly adjusted axis-limits.

 This plot has a lot of excess space.

 Proposed solution

The following is a quick solution that seems to work. But it may be possible to make a better solution when integrating it into the hist2d function. It should be made as an optional argument such as hist2d(adapt_lim=True, ...) to adapt both x and y-axis, or specify a given axis such as hist2d(adapt_lim='x', ...) 

I don't really have time to add this to Matplotlib's code-base myself, and make sure everything is made according to your standards etc. So hopefully someone else can do it, if you like the feature. Thanks!

 Plot 2-dim histogram and get bins and edges.
 h, xedges, yedges, _ = plt.hist2d(x, y, bins=100, cmin=20);

 mask = ~np.isnan(h)

 mask_flat_x = np.any(mask, axis=1)
 mask_flat_y = np.any(mask, axis=0)

 Get x-axis min/max for bins that are actually used.
 x_min = xedges[:-1][mask_flat_x].min()

 y_min = yedges[:-1][mask_flat_y].min()
 y_max = yedges[1:][mask_flat_y].max()

 Adjust x-axis limits to have a little padding.
 x_pad = 0.01 (x_max - x_min)
 plt.xlim(x_min - x_pad, x_max + x_pad)

 y_pad = 0.01 (y_max - y_min)

### Problem

Plotting a 2-dim histogram using the `hist2d` function can leave a lot of excess space in the plot when using the argument `cmin` to exclude bins with insufficient numbers of data-points. (There's presumably a similar problem when using the argument `cmax`).

    %matplotlib inline
    import numpy as np
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    # Generate random x/y values.
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1234)
    size = 100000
    x = rng.normal(scale=10, size=size)
    y = rng.normal(size=size)

    # This plot has properly adjusted axis-limits.
    plt.hist2d(x, y, bins=100, cmin=1);

![image](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/assets/13588114/f9d89963-89f3-4cf1-86dd-55ff4efed47e)

    # This plot has a lot of excess space.
    plt.hist2d(x, y, bins=100, cmin=20);

![image](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/assets/13588114/2df600a7-d988-466a-83f4-5bc7c3cf19c7)


### Proposed solution

The following is a quick solution that seems to work. But it may be possible to make a better solution when integrating it into the `hist2d` function. It should be made as an optional argument such as `hist2d(adapt_lim=True, ...)` to adapt both x and y-axis, or specify a given axis such as `hist2d(adapt_lim='x', ...)` 

I don't really have time to add this to Matplotlib's code-base myself, and make sure everything is made according to your standards etc. So hopefully someone else can do it, if you like the feature. Thanks!

    # Plot 2-dim histogram and get bins and edges.
    h, xedges, yedges, _ = plt.hist2d(x, y, bins=100, cmin=20);

    # Boolean mask whether a bin is actually used in the 2-dim grid.
    mask = ~np.isnan(h)

    # Flattened boolean masks whether a bin is actually used for each axis.
    mask_flat_x = np.any(mask, axis=1)
    mask_flat_y = np.any(mask, axis=0)

    # Get x-axis min/max for bins that are actually used.
    x_min = xedges[:-1][mask_flat_x].min()
    x_max = xedges[1:][mask_flat_x].max()

    # Get y-axis min/max for bins that are actually used.
    y_min = yedges[:-1][mask_flat_y].min()
    y_max = yedges[1:][mask_flat_y].max()

    # Adjust x-axis limits to have a little padding.
    x_pad = 0.01 * (x_max - x_min)
    plt.xlim(x_min - x_pad, x_max + x_pad)

    # Adjust y-axis limits to have a little padding.
    y_pad = 0.01 * (y_max - y_min)
    plt.ylim(y_min - y_pad, y_max + y_pad)

    plt.show();

![image](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/assets/13588114/c22e7bbb-5666-41f8-bda4-28229a297d16)
kept_issues.title: [ENH]: Adapt 2-dim histogram axis limits to content

Problem

The supxlabel() and supylabel() functions are very useful to label the axes of multiple subplots. But it is often ungainly that the labels are centred on the figure, and not on the axes of the plot.

kept_issues.body:
### Problem

The `supxlabel()` and `supylabel()` functions are very useful to label the axes of multiple subplots. But it is often ungainly that the labels are centred on the figure, and not on the axes of the plot.

![image](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/assets/3993688/4dc7607c-794f-4f18-9eb3-a83e244e07b4)

It would be great if a parameter, say, could be added to the functions that centres the labels on the axes instead.

### Proposed solution

Here's a very simple toy implementation, using the bounding boxes of `Figure.axes`.

```py
class AxesBbox(BboxBase):
    def __init__(self, axes):
        super().__init__()
        self._points = None
        self._bboxes = [ax.bbox for ax in axes]
        self.set_children(*self._bboxes)

    def get_points(self):
        if self._invalid:
            self._points = self.union(self._bboxes).get_points()
            self._invalid = 0
        return self._points


def supxlabel(fig, *args, **kwargs):
    label = fig.supxlabel(*args, **kwargs)
    trans = blended_transform_factory(BboxTransformTo(AxesBbox(fig.axes)),
                                      label.get_transform())
    label.set_transform(trans)
    return label


def supylabel(fig, *args, **kwargs):
    label = fig.supylabel(*args, **kwargs)
    trans = blended_transform_factory(label.get_transform(),
                                      BboxTransformTo(AxesBbox(fig.axes)))
    label.set_transform(trans)
    return label

```

![image](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/assets/3993688/f1ab17f3-1509-4902-a750-8d561f682e24)
kept_issues.title: [ENH]: Add option to centre `supxlabel()` and `supylabel()` on axes

kept_issues.body:
### Problem

I often have a list of `n` things to plot in different subplots, and I want to create subplots automatically that have an as-square-as-possible layout. For example, if I have 2-3 subplots, I only want 1 row, if I have 4-8, I want 2 rows of 2-4, if I have 9, I want 3x3, etc.
Additionally, the default figsize should scale with the number of figures.

### Proposed solution

Full solution including MWE:
```
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(-1,1,100)
powers = {i: x**i for i in range(7)}

# Solution #########
n = len(powers)
n_rows = int(n // np.sqrt(n))
n_cols = int(np.ceil(n / n_rows))
figwidth_default = min(15, 4 * n_cols)
figheight_default = min(8, 1 + 3 * n_rows)
figsize = (figwidth_default, figheight_default)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(n_rows, n_cols, figsize=figsize, layout="constrained")
################

for ax, (name, power) in zip(axes.flatten(), powers.items()):
    ax.plot(x, power)
    ax.set_title(f"x^{name}")
plt.show()
```

### Problem

In matplotlib, colormaps are callable but `ScalarMappables` are not callable. However, adding a colorbar to a figure requires a `ScalarMappable`. It would be useful to make `ScalarMappable` callable (for convenience) so they can be used interchangeably with colormap objects. This way, a user that wants to make a colorbar from a colormap doesn't need to use the second step of making a `ScalarMappable`, they can just use a `ScalarMappable` from the beginning. 


### Proposed solution

`ScalarMappables` already have the method called ``to_rgba(x, alpha=None, bytes=False, norm=True)``. So this feature request would be as simple as adding a ``__call__`` method that has identical inputs and deploys ``to_rgba()``.

```
def __call__(self, x, alpha=None, bytes=False, norm=True):
        """
        Return a normalized RGBA array corresponding to *x*.
        This is a convenience function that is identical to ``to_rgba``. For 
        more information, see the documentation for that method. 
        """
        return self.to_rgba(x, alpha=alpha, bytes=bytes, norm=norm)
```

kept_issues.body:
### Problem

## Lack of forward consistency in the recommended replacement for a deprecated method
``matplotlib.cm.get_cmap()`` is deprecated. The recommended replacement is ``matplotlib.colormaps.get_cmap`` or ``matplotlib.colormaps[<name>]``. However, these replacements do not have the option to automatically resample the colormap using an optional input argument `lut`, like ``cm.get_cmap()`` does. 

## Example use case 
```python
import matplotlib as mpl

# Currently, users can automatically resample a colormap as follows:
N=5
jet_cmap = mpl.cm.get_cmap('jet', N)

# Once `cm.get_cmap` is fully deprecated, users will have to call `resampled` instead of using the `lut` argument:
jet_cmap = mpl.colormaps.get_cmap('jet')
jet_cmap = jet_cmap.resampled(N)
```

Is the plan for users to call ``resampled(<N>)`` themselves? Or would it be helpful to add the `lut` argument to ``matplotlib.colormaps.get_cmap``?

### Proposed solution

It seems easy enough to add the `lut` argument to the [``get_cmap()``](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/blob/v3.8.0/lib/matplotlib/cm.py#L194C30-L194C30) method of ``ColormapRegistry``.


## New code suggestion
```python
    def get_cmap(self, cmap, lut=None):
        """
        Return a color map specified through *cmap*.

        Parameters
        ----------
        cmap : str or `~matplotlib.colors.Colormap` or None

            - if a `.Colormap`, return it
            - if a string, look it up in ``mpl.colormaps``
            - if None, return the Colormap defined in :rc:`image.cmap`

        lut : int or None, default: None
             If *name* is not already a Colormap instance and *lut* is not None, the
             colormap will be resampled to have *lut* entries in the lookup table.

        Returns
        -------
        Colormap
        """
        # get the default color map
        if cmap is None:
            out_cmap = self[mpl.rcParams["image.cmap"]]

        # if the user passed in a Colormap, simply return it
        if isinstance(cmap, colors.Colormap):
            out_cmap = cmap
        if isinstance(cmap, str):
            _api.check_in_list(sorted(_colormaps), cmap=cmap)
            # otherwise, it must be a string so look it up
            out_cmap = self[cmap]
        raise TypeError(
            'get_cmap expects None or an instance of a str or Colormap . ' +
            f'you passed {cmap!r} of type {type(cmap)}'
        )

       if lut is None:
            return out_cmap
       else:
            return out_cmap.resampled(lut)
```

## Potential Issue
This could generate strange behavior in the case where the input `cmap` is already a colormap...

However, forward consistency seems valuable since the new ``colormaps.get_cmap()`` is recommended as a replacement for ``cm.get_cmap()`` but it has less functionality.

### Problem

I would like to have the options to determine how the legend should be filled, i.e. rowwise or columnwise. At the moment the rows are filled first. For example:
```
x = np.arange(0, 10)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, x, label='1')
ax.plot(x, x+1, label='2')
ax.plot(x, x+ 2, label='3')
ax.plot(x, x+3, label='4')
ax.legend(ncols=2)
plt.show()
```

The legend looks like:
| 1 | 3 |
|---|---|
| 2 | 4 |

What I would like is:
| 1 | 2 |
|---|---|
| 3 | 4 |


### Proposed solution

_Not my own solution, but found here: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/10101141/matplotlib-legend-add-items-across-columns-instead-of-down_ 

One way to implement this is to add a keyword and use this function:
```python
def flip(items, ncol):
    """
    Flips the order of items in a list by grouping them into columns.
    *used to fill columns of legends first*

    Parameters:
        items (list): The list of items to be flipped.
        ncol (int): The number of columns to group the items into.

    Returns:
        itertools.chain: A chain object containing the flipped items.

    Source:
        https://stackoverflow.com/questions/10101141/
        matplotlib-legend-add-items-across-columns-instead-of-down
    """
    return itertools.chain(*[items[i::ncol] for i in range(ncol)])

handles, labels = axs.get_legend_handles_labels()
ncol = 2
ax.legend(flip(handles, ncol), flip(labels, ncol), ncol=ncol)
````

At the moment it is a seperate function, but based on an extra keyword-argument one could check if the labels should be distributed column or row wise and use the ncol argument to change this.

### Problem

It seems to me there is no easy way to save a figure in vectorial formats n times (e.g. twice) bigger than the one created with other elements scaling up as well.

[One](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/77308083/how-to-change-figure-size-and-other-size-elements-for-a-svg-file/77311912#77311912) could suggest to scale up all elements in the rc file, but it seems really hard to do without forgetting any of it.

Another way to achieve this goal is to rely on external tools, such as `svgutils`:

```python
import svgutils.transform as sg
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

figname = 'test.svg'
scale_factor = 2

fig = plt.figure()
fig.savefig(figname)

fig = sg.fromfile(figname)
newsize = ['{}pt'.format(scale_factor * float(i.replace('pt', ''))) for i in fig.get_size()]

fig.set_size(newsize)
fig.save(figname)
```

It would be great to have such a feature directly included in `matplotlib` ! Maybe as an argument of `savefig` ?


### Proposed solution

One solution would be to integrate `svgutils` directly as a required package when installing `matplotlib`, and use it. However, it is relatively new, and I do not know for how long it will be maintained.

Another solution would be to list all parameters of the rc file that should be scaled up, and work around this ?

### Problem

`ax.stackplot()` is used for conveniently plotting stacked area plot.

The documentation says that any `**kwargs` is passed on to `ax.fill_between`.

So, it all works fine if I work with colours, but not so much with hatching pattern.

If I want to add hatching, this is what I get by default:
```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Data
cols = 10
rows = 4

data = (
    np.reshape(np.arange(0, cols, 1), (1, -1)) ** 2
    + np.reshape(np.arange(0, rows), (-1, 1))
    + np.random.random((rows, cols))*5
)

# Plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(
    figsize=(10,6),
    facecolor="white",
    layout="constrained"
)
fig.suptitle(
    "with hatching",
    fontsize=25,
    weight="bold"
)

x = range(data.shape[1])
ax.stackplot(
    x, data,
    hatch="x"
)

ax.set_xlim(0, 9)
ax.set_ylim(0, 350)
```

The outcome:
![image](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/assets/8880777/7b767630-2e72-4039-93b9-6d5cb6f53c8c)

But I would be more interested in getting something like this:
![image](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/assets/8880777/feb3e55c-ba6f-4faf-b725-3d5934721a0a)



### Proposed solution

The calling signature would be the same as before with exception that the `hatch` parameter would accept e.g. a list with `hatching` styles you want to use.

Example:
```python
ax.stackplot(
    x, data,
    hatch=["x", "\\", ".", "-"]
)
```

The example I've used above in the problem was create using the code below and in this case it varies the hatching by the density:
```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(
    figsize=(10,6),
    facecolor="white",
    layout="constrained"
)
fig.suptitle(
    "with individual hatching",
    fontsize=25,
    weight="bold"
)

x = range(data.shape[1])
stack_baseline = np.zeros((data.shape[1]))
for i, y in enumerate(data):
    ax.fill_between(
        x, stack_baseline, y+stack_baseline,
        facecolor=(1, 1, 1, 0),
        hatch="x"*(data.shape[0]-i)
    )
    stack_baseline += y

ax.set_xlim(0, 9)
ax.set_ylim(0, 350)
```

### Problem

It would be nice to specify the color of a set of violin plots in the constructor, rather than doing it afterwards for each component of the violinplot. This is usually how colors are set in matplotlib, so it would be in keeping with the general schema of matplotlib.

I can set this up as a PR if people think it's useful and makes sense for the library.

### Proposed solution

The current color selection is done [here](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/blob/v3.8.1/lib/matplotlib/axes/_axes.py#L8382). It looks like this:

```python
        # Colors.
        if mpl.rcParams['_internal.classic_mode']:
            fillcolor = 'y'
            linecolor = 'r'
        else:
            fillcolor = linecolor = self._get_lines.get_next_color()
```

The proposed enhancement would look something like this, where `color` is a new key word argument with default value `=None`.

```python
        # Colors.
        if mpl.rcParams['_internal.classic_mode']:
            fillcolor = 'y'
            linecolor = 'r'
        elif color is not None:
            fillcolor = linecolor = color 
        else:
            fillcolor = linecolor = self._get_lines.get_next_color()
```

This could even work for a sequence of colors, but a little bit more code would have to be changed.

### Problem

It took me some year to figure out, that matplotlib supports `'CN'` (e.g. `'C1'`) as color.
I tried `1` (integer), but that raises only a `ValueError: 1 is not a valid value for color` (triggered by `plt.plot(np.arange(10), color=1)`)
and when I implemented a workaround to support integers in our wrappers, a colleague asked about the difference to `'CN'`.

### Proposed solution

Current code:

https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/blob/62a5ba4d3e3ac6f32ea4c8c9e89c62381390ac9a/lib/matplotlib/colors.py#L240-L246

Suggestion:

```python
def _check_color_like(**kwargs): 
     """ 
     For each *key, value* pair in *kwargs*, check that *value* is color-like. 
     """ 
     for k, v in kwargs.items(): 
         if not is_color_like(v): 
             if isinstance(v, int) and k == "color" and v >= 0:
                 raise ValueError(
                     f"{v!r} is not a valid value for {k}.\n"
                     f"To get the N'th entry from mpl.rcParams['axes.prop_cycle'] you can use 'CN' instead of an integer.") 
             raise ValueError(f"{v!r} is not a valid value for {k}") 
```

Problem

Interpretability of 3D data can be significantly enhanced by leveraging human binocular vision through the use of stereoscopic images. This would be a super cool feature to bring into matplotlib, especially when combined with animations.

In 2D, I see this good example from (edited to make it parallel-view). To do this, you would have to offset the data a bit by its Z value to generate the effect, and give each of the side-by-side plots the data offset in opposite directions.
 

In 3D, I'm thinking of this plot which I pulled from my copy of Visualizing Data (parallel-view). I believe this would be simplest by calculating a differential rotation of the view about the origin instead of calculating offsets of the data: 
 

This idea was talked about a bit in but unlike that the idea here is not to do random-dot stereograms (stereograms by definition use a single image), but side-by-side stereoscopic plots. Also out of scope would be red-cyan 3D analglyphs.

Implementation details to keep in mind:
 In 3D we may need to tie this to focal_length.
 We should support both cross-view /cross-eyed and parallel-view conventions.
 For the two above bullets, it might be best thought of as defining the IPD / inter-pupillary distance, and allowing it to go negative for the cross-view plots.
 In 3D, it's also possible to generate offsets via translation instead of rotation of the camera about the origin - that might be easier. See the WolframCloud link below. This would require first implementing the function to set the camera location as in 
 In 2D, the focal plane should always be on the page, but we should think about where we want data to be relative to it. All underneath the page? All above the page? Equally split? Probably make this configurable.
 In 2D, if you are viewing the plots "flat" / individually, then the axis labels will be inaccurate for any data that has been offset. This could lead to misinterpretation for people who are unfamiliar with or unable to do the eye maneuvers necessary to view the plots.
 For the two above bullets, one advantage of having all the points above/below the plane of the page means that one of the plots will have no offset applied to its points, and so will have accurate axis labels.

 Proposed solution

See as an existing implementation elsewhere.

I think this may be best implemented as an external package, but want to float the idea here to get feedback.

### Problem

Interpretability of 3D data can be significantly enhanced by leveraging human binocular vision through the use of [stereoscopic images](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereoscopy). This would be a super cool feature to bring into matplotlib, especially when combined with animations.

In 2D, I see this good example from https://jmonlong.github.io/Hippocamplus/2019/11/19/stereograms-1kgp-pca-tsne/ (edited to make it parallel-view). To do this, you would have to offset the data a bit by its Z value to generate the effect, and give each of the side-by-side plots the data offset in opposite directions.
![image](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/assets/14363975/8ccc1f4c-360d-4c2c-8d98-70c2c242e06e)

In 3D, I'm thinking of this plot which I pulled from my copy of [Visualizing Data](https://www.amazon.com/Visualizing-Data-William-S-Cleveland/dp/0963488406) (parallel-view). I believe this would be simplest by calculating a differential rotation of the view about the origin instead of calculating offsets of the data: 
![image](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/assets/14363975/2cf019c4-067a-425b-a822-f5c2ca55112c)

This idea was talked about a bit in https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/issues/14578, but unlike that the idea here is not to do [random-dot stereograms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autostereogram) (stereograms by definition use a single image), but side-by-side stereoscopic plots. Also out of scope would be [red-cyan 3D analglyphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anaglyph_3D).

Implementation details to keep in mind:
* In 3D we may need to tie this to `focal_length`.
* We should support both cross-view /cross-eyed and parallel-view conventions.
* For the two above bullets, it might be best thought of as defining the IPD / inter-pupillary distance, and allowing it to go negative for the cross-view plots.
* In 3D, it's also possible to generate offsets via translation instead of rotation of the camera about the origin - that might be easier. See the WolframCloud link below. This would require first implementing the function to set the camera location as in https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/issues/26394
* In 2D, the focal plane should always be on the page, but we should think about where we want data to be relative to it. All underneath the page? All above the page? Equally split? Probably make this configurable.
* In 2D, if you are viewing the plots "flat" / individually, then the axis labels will be inaccurate for any data that has been offset. This could lead to misinterpretation for people who are unfamiliar with or unable to do the eye maneuvers necessary to view the plots.
* For the two above bullets, one advantage of having all the points above/below the plane of the page means that one of the plots will have no offset applied to its points, and so will have accurate axis labels.

### Proposed solution

See https://resources.wolframcloud.com/FunctionRepository/resources/Stereogram3D as an existing implementation elsewhere.

I think this may be best implemented as an external package, but want to float the idea here to get feedback.
kept_issues.title: [ENH]: 2D / 3D stereoscopic plots

### Problem

Lots of requests for colormapping unitized data, such as #7383,  #25062, #23991,  #19476, #17447

### Proposed solution

Since the number -> number that can be colormapped conversion is done in the norm, proposing that we make an explicit Norm for handling units:

### `UnitizedNorm`:

Create a new norm object `UnitizedNorm`:

  * maps data to numbers using `{Convertor}.convert` 
  * labels colorbar using the formatters from `{Convertor}.axisinfo`

The hard work here is integrating this into the existing color-mapping pipeline, particularly the interpolation pipeline. One approach may be to add a flag indicating whether the unit can participate in existing schemes or whether it provides its own interpolation methods. If this works, then `.UnitizedNorm` can be shimmed in to act as an analogue to `NoNorm`

### `UnitizedNorm(Normalize)`

I don't know if this is actually possible, or remotely worth the effort given @ksunden's work, but a follow on proposal is that  `UnitizedNorm` acts as a wrapper around `Normalize` objects so that the norms can take in unitized inputs, where `UnitizedNorm(NoNorm) == UnitizedNorm()` is the default described above. The objective would be to allow support for things like 
`UnitizedNorm(BoundaryNorm(['2011-01-01', '2011-02-01', '2011-03-01']))' or "UnitizedNorm(Normalize(vmin=Pint(10))" 

Pretty sure that if this is possible, it ends up being some sorta dynamic monkeypatching of the existing class. But also if possible then it can be written as a decorator and that would be nice to have for custom Norms.

### Problem

Hello, 

I am integrating Matplotlib with the QtBackend inside a tool of data analysis.
I would be interested if the function save_figure from the NavigationToolbar2QT class could return the fullpath of the saved image (the variable fname).
For now I have overloaded this function by adding the return parameter but it would much neater if it was made directly inside matplotlib. Plus, this could interest other people. 

For consistency, maybe it would be best to do that for all backends. 

What do you think ?

### Proposed solution

The function would look like this : 

```python

    def save_figure(self, *args):
        filetypes = self.canvas.get_supported_filetypes_grouped()
        sorted_filetypes = sorted(filetypes.items())
        default_filetype = self.canvas.get_default_filetype()

        startpath = os.path.expanduser(mpl.rcParams['savefig.directory'])
        start = os.path.join(startpath, self.canvas.get_default_filename())
        filters = []
        selectedFilter = None
        for name, exts in sorted_filetypes:
            exts_list = " ".join(['*.%s' % ext for ext in exts])
            filter = f'{name} ({exts_list})'
            if default_filetype in exts:
                selectedFilter = filter
            filters.append(filter)
        filters = ';;'.join(filters)

        fname, filter = QtWidgets.QFileDialog.getSaveFileName(
            self.canvas.parent(), "Choose a filename to save to", start,
            filters, selectedFilter)
        if fname:
            # Save dir for next time, unless empty str (i.e., use cwd).
            if startpath != "":
                mpl.rcParams['savefig.directory'] = os.path.dirname(fname)
            try:
                self.canvas.figure.savefig(fname)
            except Exception as e:
                QtWidgets.QMessageBox.critical(
                    self, "Error saving file", str(e),
                    QtWidgets.QMessageBox.StandardButton.Ok,
                    QtWidgets.QMessageBox.StandardButton.NoButton)
        return fname
```

Problem

Currently, boxplots do not get legend entries. 27711 was an attempt to introduce them but only solved one very particular usecase and did not generalize well. See 

There is a labels parameter, but that only sets x-tick labels. And it has one entry per box. For the legend we should have only one entry per boxplot() call no matter how many boxes that has, because boxplot draws N identically styled boxes and it does not make sense to have N identical handles with different labels.

Because of the x-tick relation of labels and it's relation to individual boxes, this parameter is not suited for the legend labels. 

 Proposed solution

We need a separate parameter. There are basically two options:

 Variant 1) legend_label: str

pro: simple and clear, no interference with the existing API
con: inconsistent with the rest of the library: all other functions use label for the legend entry.

 Variant 2) label: str
pro: consistent with the rest of the library
con: Having label alongside labels is quite confusing and easily leads to errors. (We could runtime-check for the type str vs list of str, to give helpful error messages but still ...)
If we want to go this way, we should rename labels to tick_labels or similar.
kept_issues.body:
### Problem

Currently, boxplots do not get legend entries. #27711 was an attempt to introduce them but only solved one very particular usecase and did not generalize well. See https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/pull/27780.

There is a `labels` parameter, but that only sets x-tick labels. And it has one entry per box. For the legend we should have only one entry per `boxplot()` call no matter how many boxes that has, because `boxplot` draws N identically styled boxes and it does not make sense to have N identical handles with different labels.

Because of the x-tick relation of  `labels` and it's relation to individual boxes, this parameter is not suited for the legend labels. 

### Proposed solution

We need a separate parameter. There are basically two options:

#### Variant 1) `legend_label: str`

*pro*: simple and clear, no interference with the existing API
*con*: inconsistent with the rest of the library: all other functions use `label` for the legend entry.


#### Variant 2) `label: str`
*pro*: consistent with the rest of the library
*con*: Having `label` alongside `labels` is quite confusing and easily leads to errors. (We could runtime-check for the type str vs list of str, to give helpful error messages but still ...)
If we want to go this way, we should rename `labels` to `tick_labels` or similar.
